title: The Corner Is in the Government's Argument; the Holding Company Is in the Judgment
participants: Attorney General of the United States
Supreme Court of the United States

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The skim is the exchange ratio, and the Court describes it without pricing it: shareholders of the two railroads were to "receive, upon an agreed basis of value, shares in the holding corporation". What that basis was, and who set it, is not in the opinion.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was jurisdictional. The two railroads were "corporations having competing and substantially parallel lines from the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River to the Pacific Ocean at Puget Sound", and the device chosen to end their competition was "a corporation, under the laws of New Jersey, which should hold the shares of the stock of the constituent companies" — a Minnesota and Washington problem solved by a New Jersey charter.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The fog is the only part of the May 1901 corner the case preserves, and it survives in the Attorney General's argument rather than in the Court's findings. On the Government's account, "those in control of the Union Pacific attempted to acquire control of the Northern Pacific and as soon as Mr. Hill and Mr. Morgan heard of this attempt they reached an understanding to oppose it in concert" — two blocs buying the same shares, neither disclosing, in a market that had no way to see that the float was being bought twice.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall is what the holding company held: "more than nine-tenths of the stock of the Northern Pacific, and more than three-fourths of the stock of the Great Northern". The Court's finding on what that meant is categorical — the constituent companies "ceased, under this arrangement, to be in active competition for trade and commerce along their respective lines, and became, practically, one powerful consolidated corporation, by the name of a holding corporation".
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: This is the stage the case denies to the pattern, and the dossier records it as a denial. There was no settlement and no inquiry report: the arrangement "was an illegal combination in restraint of interstate commerce and fell within the prohibitions and provisions of the act of July 2, 1890", and the Circuit Court's injunction was upheld — the holding company restrained "from voting such stock and from exercising any control whatever over the acts and doings of the railroad companies", the railroads restrained from paying it dividends. The remedy was structural and it was granted. What it was not was criminal; as the Attorney General said, "The contention as to whether the Anti-Trust Act is or is not a criminal statute is not material."

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The New Jersey holding-company charter, and the prior attempt at the same end that had already been struck down — the transfer of half the Northern Pacific's stock to the Great Northern in exchange for a bond guarantee, "held to be violative of the laws of Minnesota, Pearsall v. Great Northern Ry. Co., 161 U. S. 646".
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: A Sherman Act holding that a holding company is a combination, reached without any criminal charge — the equitable injunction as the instrument of antitrust, which is the form the next sixty years of the statute took.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: A contest for control destabilises the market; the truce that settles it concentrates the two contestants' holdings in one vehicle; the vehicle is then the thing the law has to attack. The Government's own argument describes the pattern repeating: "On at least three prior occasions Mr. [Hill] and Mr. Morgan and their associates acted in concert in transactions affecting both roads."

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the Supreme Court tried and condemned the Northern Pacific corner of May 1901 — that the great panic was adjudicated, and the men who engineered it were held to account for it.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: It did not happen. The panic of May 1901 appears in this case exactly once, in the ARGUMENT OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL FOR THE UNITED STATES, offered as one of three occasions evidencing concert between Hill and Morgan — alongside the Pearsall transfer and "the joint purchase of the Burlington in 1901". It is not in the syllabus, it is not the subject of any holding, and no finding is made about it. What the Court decided was the lawfulness of the company formed out of the TRUCE that ended the corner: a New Jersey holding corporation taking in over nine-tenths of one railroad and over three-quarters of the other. The remedy was an injunction against voting the stock, in a civil action in equity. Nobody was charged with cornering anything; no trader's loss is quantified anywhere in the opinion; and the short sellers caught in May 1901 — the people the legend is about — are not before the court and are not mentioned. The record is also physically imperfect: this is OCR of a scanned 1904 volume, and its errors are visible enough to be worth stating (the running head reads "NORTHERN SECIJRIITIES CO. v. UNiITED STATES" and Hill's name appears once as "Mr. Ill"), which is why no figure is taken from it.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Northern Securities Company v. United States, 193 U.S. 197, decided 14 March 1904. Held: stockholders of the Great Northern and Northern Pacific, companies with competing and substantially parallel lines to Puget Sound, combined to organise a New Jersey holding corporation to hold their shares; that corporation came to hold more than nine-tenths of the Northern Pacific's stock and more than three-quarters of the Great Northern's; the constituent companies necessarily ceased to be in active competition and became practically one consolidated corporation under a holding company's name; the arrangement was an illegal combination in restraint of interstate commerce within the Act of 2 July 1890; and the Circuit Court had power to enjoin the holding company from voting the stock or exercising any control over the railroads, and the railroads from paying it dividends. Separately, and only in the Government's argument, the events leading to the panic of May 1901 are described as evidence of concert: after the Union Pacific was refused an interest in the Burlington purchase, its controllers moved on the Northern Pacific; Hill and Morgan, on hearing of it, agreed to oppose it in concert; this led to the threat to retire the Northern Pacific's preferred stock and to the conference at which the plan announced on 1 June was arranged.

citations.title: Northern Securities Company v. United States, 193 U.S. 197 (argued 14–15 December 1903, decided 14 March 1904) — United States Reports, volume 193
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the Library of Congress's United States Reports collection (7.3 MB) and read as extracted text. THE TEXT IS OCR OF A SCANNED VOLUME AND CONTAINS VISIBLE ERRORS — the running head reads "NORTHERN SECIJRIITIES CO. v. UNiITED STATES", "the custodian" appears as "tile custodian", and James J. Hill's name appears in one passage as "Mr. Ill". Nothing is quoted here that depends on a doubtful character, and no figure is taken from this scan. THE HOLDING, from the syllabus: stockholders of the Great Northern and Northern Pacific — "corporations having competing and substantially parallel lines from the Great Lakes and the Mississippi River to the Pacific Ocean at Puget Sound" — "combined and conceived the scheme of organizing a corporation, under the laws of New Jersey, which should hold the shares of the stock of the constituent companies". The holding corporation came to hold "more than nine-tenths of the stock of the Northern Pacific, and more than three-fourths of the stock of the Great Northern". The Court held "that, necessarily, the constituent companies ceased, under this arrangement, to be in active competition for trade and commerce along their respective lines, and became, practically, one powerful consolidated corporation, by the name of a holding corporation", and "that the arrangement was an illegal combination in restraint of interstate commerce and fell within the prohibitions and provisions of the act of July 2, 1890" — the Sherman Act. The remedy upheld was an injunction restraining the holding company "from voting such stock and from exercising any control whatever over the acts and doings of the railroad companies", and the railroads from paying it dividends. WHAT THE CASE SAYS ABOUT THE MAY 1901 CORNER, AND WHERE IT SAYS IT. The panic appears in the ARGUMENT OF THE ATTORNEY GENERAL FOR THE UNITED STATES, not in the Court's holding. The Government argued that on "at least three prior occasions" Hill and Morgan "and their associates acted in concert in transactions affecting both roads", listing the attempted stock transfer struck down in Pearsall v. Great Northern Ry. Co., 161 U.S. 646, "the joint purchase of the Burlington in 1901", and "the events leading up to the panic of May, 1901". Its account of those events: "After the refusal to admit the Union Pacific to an interest in the Burlington purchase, those in control of the Union Pacific attempted to acquire control of the Northern Pacific and as soon as Mr. Hill and Mr. Morgan heard of this attempt they reached an understanding to oppose it in concert, and this resulted in the threat to retire the preferred stock of the Northern Pacific, and the subsequent conference at which the plan announced in the statement of June 1, in the Wall Street Summary, was arranged." The Government concluded that "the incorporation of the Securities Company, and its acquisition of a large majority of the stock of both railway companies were the designed results of a plan or understanding between the defendants Hill and Morgan and their associates, which was carried out to the letter by the parties thereto." SO THE LIMIT IS PRECISE: this is the Supreme Court holding unlawful the company formed out of the truce that ended the corner. It does not adjudicate the corner. Nobody is charged here with cornering a stock, no trader's losses are quantified, and the case is civil and in equity throughout — as the Attorney General put it, "The contention as to whether the Anti-Trust Act is or is not a criminal statute is not material."
